common_name: Fleurel Dahlia (Classic Pure White Waterlily Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Fleurel is a long-standing waterlily-class favorite, opening pure white, shallow-petaled blooms with a faint ivory cast at the center that float above the foliage on wiry stems. The flat, broad-petaled form sheds rain better than fully double decoratives and stays crisp through hot spells. A single stake is usually enough to keep the slender stems upright once buds open. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep the plant producing fresh flowers for cutting through the season.

common_name: Shea's Rainbow Dahlia (Bicolor Pink-and-Yellow Waterlily Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Shea's Rainbow carries shallow waterlily-form blooms that blend soft pink and golden yellow within the same flower, each petal shading differently so no two blooms look quite alike. The open, flat-petaled form holds up well in humid weather and rarely balls up after rain. Stake the stems lightly where wind is an issue, since the broad flowers can catch a breeze. Pinch the central growing tip early in the season to promote a bushier, more floriferous plant.

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Noreen produces small, perfectly round pompon blooms in a rich purple-red, each one tightly quilled from center to edge in the honeycomb pattern that defines the class. The dense, ball-like flowers sit on strong stems that rarely need individual staking, though a ring of twine around the clump helps in windy gardens. Pinch out the growing tip when plants are young to build a bushier framework and more flowering stems. Disbud the side shoots near each stem tip if larger, more uniform pompons are wanted for cutting or show.

common_name: Vera Higgins Dahlia (Bronze-Foliage Apricot-Orange Anemone Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Vera Higgins pairs dark bronze-purple foliage with anemone-form flowers whose flat outer ray petals surround a dense, pincushion-like center of tubular apricot-orange florets. The bicolor contrast between dusky leaves and warm-toned blooms makes this an old favorite for mixed borders. Stake the stems in exposed sites, since the foliage color comes with a slightly looser habit than green-leaved bedding types. Lift and store tubers over winter where temperatures drop below the mid-20s Fahrenheit.

common_name: Honka Surprise Dahlia (Soft Yellow Star-Form Orchid Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Honka Surprise opens narrow, spidery, star-shaped petals in a soft butter yellow around a small open eye, giving an airy, informal look quite different from the dense doubles of decorative dahlias. The light, open flowers are held well above the foliage on long stems, making them useful for loose cut arrangements. Plants branch freely, so a single central stake plus light corralling is usually enough support. Deadhead regularly, since this type sets seed readily and spent blooms slow new bud production.

common_name: Honka Fragile Dahlia (Pale Lemon Star-Form Orchid Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Honka Fragile is a paler sibling of the Honka star-form group, its narrow, well-spaced petals washed in the lightest lemon with a greenish cast near the open center. The delicate, lacy flowers move easily in a breeze and read as almost translucent in bright sun. Give plants a light stake or let them lean into neighboring perennials for informal support. Cut stems for arrangements early in the morning while blooms are freshest and least likely to shatter.

common_name: Bishop's Children Dahlia (Mixed-Color Dark-Foliage Seed Strain)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-8 weeks before the last frost; transplant out once danger of frost has passed.

directions: Bishop's Children is an open-pollinated seed strain derived from the species behind the Bishop of Llandaff line, producing a mix of single and semi-double blooms in reds, oranges, pinks, and yellows above dark bronze-to-black foliage. Because it comes true from seed rather than division, each plant in a packet varies slightly in bloom color while sharing the same dusky leaf color and airy habit. Stake the taller stems in open sites and pinch young plants once to encourage bushier growth. Where winters drop below the mid-20s Fahrenheit, lift and store the tuberous roots or simply treat the strain as an annual and resow.

common_name: Gallery Cezanne Dahlia (Dwarf Deep Red Patio Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 3-4 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; well suited to containers.

directions: Gallery Cezanne is a compact patio-type decorative dahlia bred for pots, bearing fully double, deep red blooms that look oversized for its short, bushy frame. The low, mounded habit needs no staking in containers and holds up well against summer wind on a patio or balcony. Deadhead spent flowers promptly to keep the naturally free-flowering plant producing new buds. In cold climates, bring potted tubers indoors or lift and store them once foliage is killed by frost.

common_name: Gallery Rembrandt Dahlia (Dwarf Golden-Orange Patio Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 3-4 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; well suited to containers.

directions: Gallery Rembrandt packs fully double, golden-orange decorative blooms onto a short, dense plant bred for small gardens and patio pots. The sturdy, compact stems carry the comparatively large flowers without flopping, so no staking is needed in a container or border edge. Shelter from the harshest midday sun in hot climates helps hold the warm color without fading. Lift and store tubers over winter, or discard and replant fresh tubers each spring where space is limited.

common_name: Mystic Haze Dahlia (Dark-Foliage Lavender-Pink Single Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Mystic Haze belongs to the dark-leaved Mystic group, pairing near-black bronze foliage with soft lavender-pink single blooms that glow against the dusky leaves. The open, daisy-like flowers attract pollinators readily and keep coming in flushes through summer and fall. The compact habit stands on its own in a border or large container without staking. Deadhead to extend bloom and lift tubers before hard frost in colder zones.

common_name: Happy Single Princess Dahlia (Dark-Foliage Cream-White Single Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Happy Single Princess carries creamy white single flowers with a soft blush at the petal base over dark bronze-green foliage, part of the same bedding-dahlia group as its 'Happy Single' siblings. The free-branching, compact plants bloom continuously and need no staking in beds or containers. Open-faced flowers draw bees and butterflies throughout the season. Deadhead to keep new buds forming, and lift tubers for winter storage where the ground freezes.

common_name: Karma Naomi Dahlia (Soft Peach-Apricot Cut-Flower Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Karma Naomi is part of the Karma series bred specifically for the cut-flower trade, producing fully double decorative blooms in a soft peach-apricot blend on long, straight, sturdy stems. Flowers hold exceptionally well once cut, a trait bred into the whole Karma line for the florist market. A single stake per plant keeps the strong stems from leaning once blooms reach full size. Harvest when outer petals are fully open but the center is still tight for the longest vase life.

common_name: Karma Thalia Dahlia (Orange Cut-Flower Waterlily Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Karma Thalia bears vivid orange, shallow waterlily-form blooms on the long, straight stems the Karma cut-flower series was bred for. The flat-petaled flowers resist bruising in transport better than deeper decorative types, making this a market-grower favorite. Give plants a single stake and corral stems loosely as the clump fills in. Cut when blooms are three-quarters open for the best balance of vase life and display.

common_name: Karma Fuchsiana Dahlia (Deep Pink-Magenta Cut-Flower Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Karma Fuchsiana produces fully double, deep pink-magenta decorative blooms bred into the long-stemmed Karma cut-flower line for commercial and home cutting gardens alike. The saturated color and tidy bloom form hold up well both in the garden and in the vase. Stake each stem individually once flowering begins, since the heavy heads can nod on lax growth. Lift and store tubers in autumn where winters bring hard freezes.
